extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, managers, CSR practitioners, policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic overview of corporate social responsibility (CSR): definitions, approaches, implementation practices, reporting frameworks, common initiatives, and debates about CSR's business and social impacts. Useful as a reference for practitioners, students, and policymakers seeking the field's main dimensions and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of corporate social responsibility (CSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR refers to companies conducting their core operations in a responsible and sustainable way to create a positive corporate social impact; a form of international private business self-regulation which aims to contribute to societal and environmental goals by reducing harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the working definition throughout the article. Emphasises responsibility across production, employment and investment, and notes CSR can be philanthropic or strategic. Explains variations in definition by disciplinary perspective (business, NGO, government).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic CSR
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic CSR is a long-term approach to creating a net positive social impact based on brand alignment, stakeholder integration, and ethical behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as embedding CSR strategically in the company to potentially improve firm performance; contrasted with ad-hoc philanthropy. Guidance implies alignment with company strategy/brand and use of market position to create impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating Shared Value (CSV)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Creating shared value" is an extension of CSR which allows for social obligations to be met while the company reaps a profit, acknowledging trade-offs but finding competitive advantage by building social value into strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CSV emphasises creating business opportunities linked to social problems; note that CSV tends to focus on shareholders and consumers as essential stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's pyramid of responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Carroll described CSR as a pyramid of responsibilities: economic, legal, ethical, and philanthropic responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a classification of CSR activities rather than a strict definition. Suggests companies have layered responsibilities, from making profit to meeting ethical and philanthropic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder perspective views CSR primarily through obligations to multiple stakeholders (consumers, employees, investors, communities, etc.); a review of many articles found stakeholder perspective is the most prevalent dimension of CSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies CSR evaluation should consider impact across all relevant stakeholders. Cites Business Dictionary definition listing waste reduction, contributing educational/social programs, and earning adequate returns as expressions of CSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple bottom line (people, planet, profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The triple bottom line evaluates CSR across three dimensions: 'People' (fair labour practices, community), 'Planet' (sustainable environmental practices), and 'Profit' (economic value created after full costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one way to evaluate CSR; guidance notes balancing economic, ecological, and social goals and also lists criticisms (selectivity, lack of standard auditing procedure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six types of corporate social initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR includes six types of corporate social initiatives: Corporate philanthropy; Community volunteering; Socially-responsible business practices; Cause promotions and activism; Cause-related marketing; Corporate social marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which of these are typically profit-motivated (cause marketing, activism) vs. non-profit-motivated (philanthropy, volunteering). Notes only some activities rise to the level of cause marketing (dual purpose: profitability and social benefit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep CSR / Truly Responsible Enterprise (TRE) principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep CSR describes a 'Truly Responsible Enterprise' that: sees itself as part of the system (not profit-only), recognises unsustainability as a major challenge, accepts businesses must work on solutions according to economic weight, honestly evaluates its role in problems (focus on 2–3 main problems), and takes essential systematic steps toward sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five TRE principles are: minimal transport; maximal fairness; zero economism; maximum middle size; product/service falling to the most sustainable 30%. Intended as guidance for deeper systemic CSR embedding, especially in SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit analysis / Resource-Based View (RBV) for CSR
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cost–benefit analysis and RBV to assess CSR investments: sustainable competitive advantage requires resources that are valuable (V), rare (R), inimitable (I) and non-substitutable (S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers can decide CSR investment levels like other investments; a CSR-based strategy only sustains high returns if it cannot be imitated. Literature caveats noted (innovation may drive financial performance rather than CSR itself).

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR and corporate financial performance measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical research evaluates the relationship between CSR policies and corporate financial performance using proxies (e.g., return on assets) and regression analysis; studies report positive, negative, and neutral effects depending on specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mixed evidence and methodological sensitivity; notes some studies find a positive link while others caution that innovation or flawed empirical approaches can change conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of CSR (including supply chain and product lifecycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR scope goes beyond the firm to include supplier behaviour, uses to which products are put, disposal after value loss, brand citizenship, and even 'unincorporated market behaviour'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages broader consideration (supply chains, brand perception, informal/illegal activities) when evaluating CSR; warns focusing only on identifiable firm actions risks missing important sources of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply chain CSR / responsible procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply chain CSR requires responsible procurement practices, avoiding child/forced labour, conducting social and environmental audits of suppliers, supporting fair trade, and improving visibility across the supply chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples of reputational harms (Savar building collapse, horsemeat scandal) and recommends including social responsibility in component quality reviews and using technology to improve supply-chain visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarking: review competitor initiatives, measure and evaluate the impact of those policies on society and the environment, and assess how others perceive competitor CSR strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by companies to assess their CSR policy, implementation and effectiveness; provides comparative insight to set targets and learn from peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social accounting, auditing and reporting (CSR reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social accounting is the communication of social and environmental effects of a company's economic actions to interest groups and society; emphasises corporate accountability and development of appropriate measures and reporting techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern CSR uses many standards, frameworks and metrics; no single fixed standard exists. Reporting should identify socially relevant behaviour, determine accountability audiences, and develop measures and techniques for disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standards, frameworks and indices
rubrics_metrics.description: A range of reporting guidelines and standards serve as frameworks for social accounting and reporting: AccountAbility AA1000; The Prince's Connected Reporting Framework; Fair Labor Association audits; Fair Wear Foundation verification; Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Sustainability Reporting Guidelines; Economy for the Common Good balance sheet; GoodCorporation standard; ISO 26000; SRSCMS; Earthcheck; SA8000; Standard Ethics Aei; ISO 14000; United Nations Global Compact (Communication on Progress); ISAR guidance; FTSE4Good Index; EthicalQuote (CEQ); Islamic Reporting Initiative (IRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists frameworks and explains that some countries (e.g., France) have legal reporting requirements. Notes variability across reports and criticisms that some reports amount to lip service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and third‑party assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers and stakeholders should verify CSR claims using accounting, auditing and reporting resources; third-party verifiers include Forest Stewardship Council, International Cocoa Initiative, Kimberly Process, United Nations Global Compact frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification resources provide foundation for consumers to confirm social sustainability; industries have specific verification resources and voluntary/mandatory reporting/verification arrangements vary by jurisdiction and sector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement plan for CSR communication
rubrics_metrics.description: An engagement plan helps reach the desired audience: CSR teams should plan goals and objectives, define a budget to demonstrate commitment, and scale programs appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clearly defined engagement plan is recommended to set targets, allocate resources, and show organisational commitment; budget signals relative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation: organisational placement and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR may be based within HR, business development, PR, or a separate unit reporting to the CEO or board of directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of placement affects visibility, accountability, and strategic integration; governance through senior leadership can signal higher commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics training
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics training inside corporations aims to help employees make ethical decisions when answers are unclear and is sometimes required by regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training reduces likelihood of breaches, fines and reputational harm, and can increase employee loyalty and pride. It is presented as a spreading mechanism for CSR within organisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common CSR actions (practical activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common CSR actions include environmental sustainability (recycling, waste management, water management, renewable energy, greener supply chains, LEED standards), human capital enhancement (training, education), community involvement (charity, volunteering, local employment), ethical marketing, and supply-chain management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples of activities to implement CSR; notes that not all CSR activities are equally attractive to consumers and alignment with company goals is important to avoid negative impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social licence to operate (SLO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social licence to operate refers to the level of support and approval of a company's activities by its stakeholders and communities; companies comply with societal expectations to maintain SLO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving SLO requires building trust and relationships, identifying social licence holders, measuring their intention to support, identifying negative factors, developing a Social Licence Development Strategy, and ongoing monitoring. Failure to maintain SLO can rapidly jeopardise projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for achieving Social Licence to Operate (operational steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain/maintain SLO: identify business strategy/objectives; identify social licence holders for each objective; identify desired support (target, context, timing, action); quantitatively measure intention to support; identify factors negatively impacting intention; develop strategy to remove negatives and ensure positive intention; perform ongoing monitoring and quantitative measurement of SLO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an ordered operational framework for companies to manage stakeholder support and measure changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR)
rubrics_metrics.description: CDR is an extension of CSR addressing data protection, AI ethics, digital inclusion, and the environmental impact of digital operations; typically managed by CSR departments but integration into CSR frameworks is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes national initiatives (Germany, France) and suggests CDR applies to digital business models; guidance implies CDR should be included in CSR planning and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks, criticisms and anti-patterns of CSR
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms include CSR being window-dressing or greenwash, distracting from economic role of businesses, creating unrealistic expectations, or being used to pre-empt government regulation; empirical studies show contradictory financial impacts depending on analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns practitioners to avoid superficial CSR (lip service), ensure alignment with company goals, measure social impact carefully, and be wary of reputational risk from hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CSR for recruitment and human resources
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR programs can aid recruitment and retention, particularly among graduates; involvement in CSR activities (payroll giving, volunteering) improves staff perception and customer orientation among employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests measuring employee engagement with CSR (only 31% engaged in one survey) and leveraging CSR for retention and employer branding.
